S001.title: The Board & The Rook
S001.subtitle: Meet the battlefield — and your first soldier, the mighty Rook.
S001.learning_objective: Show every legal rook move and capture from a given square, and explain why a rook can never jump over a piece.
expected_outcomes: Student can move a rook any number of empty squares in a straight line along a file or rank.
Student can capture an enemy piece with the rook by landing on its square, and knows a rook cannot jump over pieces.
Student can say which of two rooks has a clear straight line to a target square, and why the other one cannot get there.
Student is beginning to name squares with file-letter + rank-number (e.g., e4) in the warm-up naming drill — the drill returns every session, so naming is not something to master today.

concepts.primary: The rook: straight-line movement along files and ranks, and capturing by landing on an enemy piece

thinking_routine.focus: No routine yet — this is the very first lesson. We simply learn to see the board and move the rook.

materials_required: One chessboard per student (or shared online board)
A set of rooks and a few pawns (or full sets)
Coordinate stickers or a coordinate overlay for young learners (optional)

warmup_review.description: This is the first session, so there is no prior chess content to review. Instead, run a 'have you ever seen a chessboard?' opener: show the empty board and ask students what they notice (squares, two colours, a grid). This activates curiosity and surfaces what each child already knows. Keep it light and fast. Finish with the first run of the SQUARE-NAMING DRILL (about 60 seconds): call out three squares (e4, a1, h5) for the class to point to, then point at two squares and let them name the file letter and rank number. This little drill opens every session from now on, so nobody has to master naming today.

lesson_introduction.hook: Welcome to the battlefield! A chessboard is a tiny world with 64 squares. Today you meet the world — and your first soldier, the Rook, who marches in straight lines like a powerful chariot.
lesson_introduction.narrative: Tell the story of the board as a city: the up-and-down streets are called FILES (named a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h), and the side-to-side avenues are called RANKS (numbered 1 to 8). Every square has an address made of its file-letter and rank-number, just like a seat at the cinema: 'row e, number 4' becomes e4. The Rook is a chariot (or a castle tower on wheels) that can roll as far as it likes along any street or avenue — but it can never roll diagonally, and it can never jump over anyone.
lesson_introduction.description: Introduce three ideas in order: (1) files and ranks, (2) how to name a square, (3) the rook as a straight-line mover. Use the demonstration board to point at files, then ranks, then name a few squares together out loud.

key_points: FILES are the columns that go up and down, labelled a–h from White's left to right.
RANKS are the rows that go side to side, numbered 1–8 starting from White's side.
A square's name is its file-letter followed by its rank-number, e.g., d4.
The board has light and dark squares; the bottom-right square (h1) is always light ('light on right').
The ROOK moves in a straight line along its file or its rank, as many empty squares as it likes.
The rook captures by landing on an enemy piece's square — it cannot jump over any piece in its path.
core_explanation.explanation: Start with files: slide a finger up the d-file and say 'this whole street is the d-file.' Then ranks: slide along the 4th row and say 'this whole avenue is the 4th rank.' Where they cross is d4. Practise naming 4–5 squares together. Then place a single rook on an empty board and show that it 'shoots' along its file and its rank like a laser, stopping at the edge. Next, place an enemy pawn in the rook's path and show the capture: the rook travels up and lands ON the pawn's square, removing it. Finally, place a friendly piece in the path and show the rook is BLOCKED — it cannot jump. This 'blocking' idea is one of the most important rules in all of chess.

demonstrations.caption: The rook's reach on an open board.
demonstrations.explanation: Place the white rook on d4. Trace its straight lines: the whole d-file (d1–d8) and the whole 4th rank (a4–h4). Ask the class to count along with you. The rook controls a giant plus-sign (+) shape across the board.

demonstrations.caption: The rook captures by landing on the enemy.
demonstrations.explanation: White rook on d1, a black pawn on d7. The rook rolls up the empty d-file and lands on d7, removing the pawn (Rxd7). Emphasise: the rook does not 'bump' the pawn off — it takes the pawn's square and stands there.

demonstrations.caption: A rook cannot jump.
demonstrations.explanation: White rook on a1 with a friendly white pawn on a4. The rook can go to a2 or a3, but the pawn BLOCKS the rest of the a-file — the rook cannot leap over it. This is the rule that makes chess a thinking game.

guided_discussion.description: Bring students to the board and let them point and name. Ask volunteers to place a rook and show its lines, then ask the group 'where can it go?' Encourage them to spot blockers and edges. Celebrate every correct square name.
talking_points: Why is the rook called a 'straight-line' piece?
What happens when a friendly piece is in the rook's way?
What happens when an enemy piece is in the rook's way?
How is a square's name built (file first, then rank)?

questions_to_ask: Can you find the square e4 and put your finger on it?
Is the square h1 light or dark? (Always light — 'light on right'.)
If a rook is on c1, can it reach c8 if every square in between is empty?
There is a friendly pawn on c4. Can the rook on c1 reach c8 now? Why not?
There is an enemy pawn on c4. What can the rook do to it?
Show me two different squares this rook could move to — and one square it canNOT move to.

guided_examples.prompt: The rook is on d5. With your finger, trace every square it can reach. How many squares is that?
guided_examples.walkthrough: Count the d-file (d1, d2, d3, d4, d6, d7, d8 = 7 squares) and the 5th rank (a5, b5, c5, e5, f5, g5, h5 = 7 squares). The rook reaches 14 squares — a giant plus-sign. (The king on e1 is far away and does not block this rook.)
guided_examples.answer: 14 squares — 7 along the d-file and 7 along the 5th rank.

guided_examples.prompt: The rook is on d4 again. Name one square on its FILE and one square on its RANK that it can move to.
guided_examples.walkthrough: Any of d1, d2, d3, d5, d6, d7, d8 is on the file; any of a4, b4, c4, e4, f4, g4, h4 is on the rank. Have several students each name a different pair so everyone participates.
guided_examples.answer: Example: file square d8, rank square a4 (many correct answers).

prompts: What was the most important thing we learned today? Say it in your own words.
What are the two kinds of straight lines a rook can travel? (files and ranks)
What is one thing a rook is NOT allowed to do? (jump over a piece, or move diagonally)
reflection.summary_line: Today's idea in one line: The rook: straight-line movement along files and ranks, and capturing by landing on an enemy piec — and you will use it again in every game you play from here.

puzzles.prompt: White to move. There is a free black pawn. Can your rook capture it?
puzzles.explanation: The rook on d1 and the pawn on d3 share the d-file with nothing in between. The rook rolls up and lands on d3, capturing the pawn.
puzzles.educational_purpose: First capture: recognise that a rook captures along its own file by landing on the enemy.
common_mistakes: Trying to capture diagonally (rooks never move diagonally).
Stopping one square short on d2 instead of landing on the pawn.
puzzles.hint: Look straight up the d-file from the rook.

puzzles.prompt: White to move. Capture the black pawn using your rook's row (rank).
puzzles.explanation: The rook on a4 and the pawn on g4 are on the same 4th rank with empty squares between them. The rook slides right and captures on g4.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Captures happen along ranks too, not only files — the rook controls both directions.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that the rook can travel sideways as well as up and down.
puzzles.hint: Slide along the 4th rank to the right.

puzzles.prompt: White to move. The black rook is attacking your rook! Can you capture it first?
puzzles.explanation: The black rook on d2 stands right in front of your rook on d1, so your rook steps up one square and takes it. Your king is tucked away on g1 and cannot help, and nothing guards the black rook — so the rook itself wins the whole piece.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Introduce the idea that when your piece is attacked, capturing the attacker can be the best answer.
common_mistakes: Running the rook away when capturing the attacker wins a whole rook.
puzzles.hint: The enemy rook is right next door — take it!

puzzles.prompt: White to move. The black pawn is far away on the same file. Can your rook still reach it?
puzzles.explanation: The rook on a1 and the pawn on a7 share the a-file, and every square between them is empty. A rook can travel as far as it likes in one move, so it rolls all the way up to a7.
puzzles.educational_purpose: A rook's power is long range: distance does not matter as long as the path is clear.
common_mistakes: Thinking the rook can only move one or two squares.
Worrying that the pawn is 'too far' to capture.
puzzles.hint: Count the empty squares up the a-file — the path is clear all the way.

puzzles.prompt: White to move. You have TWO rooks. Only one of them can capture the pawn. Which one, and how?
puzzles.explanation: The pawn is on d4. The rook on d2 shares the d-file with it (d3 is empty), so it captures on d4. The rook on a1 cannot reach d4 in one move, so it is the wrong choice. Because only one rook can get there, we simply write Rxd4.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Choosing the right piece for the job: only the rook with a clear straight-line path can make the capture.
common_mistakes: Trying to use the a1-rook, which has no straight line to d4.
Not noticing which rook shares a file or rank with the target.
puzzles.hint: Which rook is on the same file as the pawn?

puzzles.prompt: White to move. Capture the black pawn straight up the file.
puzzles.explanation: The rook on f1 and the pawn on f5 share the f-file with empty squares between. The rook rolls up the f-file and captures on f5. The friendly king on g1 is not in the way.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Reinforce file captures and reassure students that a nearby friendly king on a different file does not block the rook.
common_mistakes: Thinking the friendly king blocks the rook (it is on the g-file, not the f-file).
puzzles.hint: The king is on g1, a different street from the rook.

puzzles.prompt: White to move. The black rook is attacking along the row. Capture it by sliding across the rank.
puzzles.explanation: The black rook on a2 and your rook on d2 are on the same 2nd rank, with c2 and b2 empty. Your rook slides left across the rank and captures on a2.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Combine 'capture the attacker' with long-range rank movement — trace the whole row before deciding.
common_mistakes: Missing that the enemy rook is reachable along the rank.
Moving the rook away instead of winning the enemy rook.
puzzles.hint: Look left along the 2nd rank — is the path to the enemy rook clear?

puzzles.prompt: White to move. The enemy rook is all the way at the top of your file. Can you capture it?
puzzles.explanation: Your rook on d1 and the black rook on d8 share the d-file, completely empty in between. Your rook travels the full file and captures on d8. As a bonus, it now attacks the black king on h8 along the 8th rank — that is called 'check', which you will learn all about soon!
puzzles.educational_purpose: Scan an entire file before deciding, and get a first, gentle glimpse of 'check' as a preview of things to come.
common_mistakes: Believing the enemy rook is too far away.
Not scanning the full length of the file.
puzzles.hint: Your rook can travel as far as the path is clear — look all the way up the d-file.

practical_activity.name: Rook Treasure Hunt
practical_activity.learning_objective: Move a rook in legal straight lines to capture targets, reinforcing files, ranks, and the no-jumping rule.
practical_activity.setup: On each student's board, place one white rook on a1 and scatter 4–6 black pawns on empty squares (the trainer can call out a setup, e.g., pawns on a5, c3, c7, f7, h3 — remember a pawn never stands on rank 1 or rank 8). No black pawn defends another; positions should allow capturing all pawns one by one.
instructions: The rook is a treasure hunter. Each black pawn is a coin.
On each turn, the student moves the rook in a straight line to capture one pawn — but only if the path is clear (no jumping!).
If a pawn is blocked by another pawn, the student must capture the blocker first. This teaches path-planning.
Naming drill: before each move, the student says the square the rook is travelling to ("c7!"). Same drill as the warm-up.
Count how many moves it takes to collect all the coins. Try again and beat your own record.
practical_activity.success_criteria: The student captures every pawn using only legal rook moves and never attempts to jump over a piece.
variations: Two-player version: players alternate, each controlling a rook on opposite corners, racing to capture the most pawns.
Naming challenge: the trainer calls out a target square and the student must find it and capture there without tracing the path with a finger first.

online_practice: Play the 'Rook' piece-movement mini-lesson or 'Knaap/Rook' practice on your academy's chosen platform (ChessKid 'Learn the Rook' or Lichess 'Piece Movement: Rook').
Complete 5 board-coordinate exercises (name-the-square) on the platform or with the printable worksheet.
over_the_board: With a parent or sibling, set up one rook and 5 pawns and play 'Rook Treasure Hunt' three times.
Practise naming 10 random squares out loud on a real board.
reflection_questions: What are the two kinds of straight lines a rook can travel? (files and ranks)
What is one thing a rook is NOT allowed to do? (jump over a piece, or move diagonally)
optional_challenge: Find the longest single rook move possible on an empty board. How many squares can a rook travel in one move? (Answer: 7.)

common_misconceptions: Confusing files and ranks — a memory aid: 'files stand up tall like filing cabinets; ranks lie down in rows like soldiers ranked side by side.'
Believing a rook can move diagonally because the queen can — stress that the rook is straight-lines only.
Thinking a capture 'pushes' a piece — clarify that the capturing piece takes over the square and the captured piece leaves the board.
typical_mistakes: Naming a square rank-first ('4e' instead of 'e4'). Gently re-order: 'letter first, then number.'
Attempting to jump a friendly piece. Re-show demonstration 3 (the blocking rook).
Moving only one square at a time, not realising the rook can travel far.
coaching_tips: Use lots of finger-tracing on the board; movement memory helps young children far more than verbal rules.
Have students SAY the square names aloud — speaking cements the coordinate system.
Keep pieces other than rooks and pawns off the board today to avoid overload; the other pieces arrive in their own sessions.
Praise the process ('great tracing!', 'you checked the whole file!') rather than just correctness.
ways_to_simplify: For very young (5-year-old) groups, use coordinate stickers around the board edge.
Reduce to file-only or rank-only movement for the first few minutes before combining.
Use the mini-game with just 3 pawns instead of 6.
extensions_for_strong_students: Ask them to find a rook path that captures all pawns in the fewest possible moves (introduces planning).
Challenge: 'Place the rook so it attacks exactly 4 of the 6 pawns at once.'
Preview question: 'If the rook attacks the enemy king, what do you think that's called?' (check).

S042.title: Fork Mastery
S042.subtitle: Spot knight forks in busy, realistic positions — and watch the fork square.
S042.learning_objective: Find knight forks in positions with more pieces, choosing a forking square the opponent cannot simply capture.
expected_outcomes: Student can find a knight fork in a busier, castled-king position.
Student knows that the forking square must be safe (e.g., not defended by the g-pawn).
Student can win a rook or queen with a forking check.
Student uses THE SCAN to find forks among many pieces.

concepts.primary: Deepening knight forks in more complex positions

thinking_routine.focus: Scan for a knight check that ALSO hits a big piece — and make sure the forking square isn't defended (watch the g-pawn!).

warmup_review.description: Recall the basic fork and THE SCAN (S034, S038). Show each briefly; one student answers; confirm. Today we find forks in busier positions.

review_items.prompt: Win the queen with a fork.

lesson_introduction.hook: You can fork on an empty board — now let's fork in a REAL game, with pawns and pieces everywhere. The skill is twofold: spot the knight check that also hits a big piece, AND make sure the enemy can't just capture your knight on the fork square. (Beware the g-pawn — it guards f6 and h6!)
lesson_introduction.narrative: Tell the class: 'Against a castled king with pawns on f7, g7, h7, the square e7 is golden — the knight checks the king from e7 and the pawns can't touch it. But f6 and h6 are guarded by the g7-pawn, so a knight there gets captured. So in busy positions, scan for a SAFE forking square. e7 forks the king with pieces on c8, c6, d5, f5, or g6.'
lesson_introduction.description: Teach finding knight forks in fuller positions and the key practical point: the forking square must be safe. Highlight e7 against the castled king and the g-pawn's guard of f6/h6.

key_points: A knight on e7 checks a king on g8 and also hits c8, c6, d5, f5, and g6.
Against pawns on f7/g7/h7, e7 is SAFE — the pawns can't capture it.
f6 and h6 are guarded by the g7-pawn, so a knight there can be taken.
Without a g7-pawn, f6 (Nf6+) becomes a strong forking square too.
Scan for a knight check that also attacks a rook or queen.
After the fork, capture the piece the opponent could not save.
core_explanation.explanation: Show the e7 fork against a castled king (demonstration 1): Ne7+ checks and wins a rook on c8 — the g-pawn can't help. Show why f6 fails when g7 is there, but works when it isn't (demonstration 2). Show a fork that wins the queen (demonstration 3). The habit: scan checks for a SAFE square that also hits a big piece.

demonstrations.caption: The golden e7 fork.
demonstrations.explanation: Ne7+ checks the king on g8 and attacks the rook on c8. The pawns on f7/g7/h7 cannot capture e7, so the fork is safe. After the king moves, Nxc8 wins the rook.

demonstrations.caption: f6 works when there's no g-pawn.
demonstrations.explanation: With no g7-pawn, Nf6+ checks the king on g8 and attacks the rook on e8 safely. (If a g7-pawn were present, it would capture on f6 — so always check the fork square is safe!)

demonstrations.caption: Forking the queen.
demonstrations.explanation: Ne7+ checks the king and attacks the queen on c8. After the king moves, Nxc8 wins the queen — a royal fork in a castled-king position.

guided_discussion.description: Show castled-king positions; students find the safe forking square (often e7) that checks the king and hits a big piece. Reinforce checking that the fork square is safe.
talking_points: Which knight square checks the king AND hits a big piece?
Is that square safe, or can a pawn capture the knight?
Why is e7 so good against pawns on f7/g7/h7?
When does f6 work, and when does it fail?

questions_to_ask: What knight check is available against the castled king?
Does that check also attack a rook or queen?
Is the forking square defended by the g-pawn?
After the king moves, what do you capture?
Did you scan for a SAFE fork?

guided_examples.prompt: Find the safe fork that wins the queen.
guided_examples.walkthrough: Ne7+ checks the king and attacks the queen on c8; the pawns can't take e7. After the king moves, Nxc8 wins the queen.

guided_examples.prompt: There's no g-pawn — find the f6 fork.
guided_examples.walkthrough: Nf6+ checks the king on g8 and attacks the rook on e8. After the king moves, Nxe8 wins the rook.

prompts: What was the most important thing we learned today? Say it in your own words.
Why is e7 such a good forking square against a castled king?
Why must you check whether the fork square is safe?
reflection.summary_line: Today's idea in one line: Deepening knight forks in more complex position — and you will use it again in every game you play from here.

puzzles.prompt: Find the safe forking check that wins the rook.
puzzles.explanation: Ne7+ forks the king on g8 and the rook on c8; the pawns can't capture e7. After the king moves, Nxc8 wins the rook.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Use the safe e7 fork against a castled king.
common_mistakes: Trying Nf6+, which the g7-pawn captures.
puzzles.hint: e7 checks the king and the pawns can't touch it.

puzzles.prompt: Find the safe fork that wins the queen.
puzzles.explanation: Ne7+ forks the king and the queen on c8; after the king moves, Nxc8 wins the queen.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Win the queen with the e7 fork.
common_mistakes: Choosing an unsafe forking square.
puzzles.hint: Check from e7 — what does it also attack?

puzzles.prompt: White to move. One move attacks two things at once. Which move, and what does it win?
puzzles.explanation: 1.Nc6+ Kc8 2.Nxd8 is the move. White wins a rook — the line is forced as far as Nxd8.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Use f6 as a forking square when it is safe.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to check whether a g-pawn guards f6.
puzzles.hint: Look for a square that touches two enemy pieces at once.
puzzles.source: pattern transform (mirror) of the original teaching position

puzzles.prompt: Find the safe fork that wins the rook on c6.
puzzles.explanation: Ne7+ forks the king on g8 and the rook on c6 (a knight on e7 attacks c6). After the king moves, Nxc6 wins the rook.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Recognise that e7 also hits c6.
common_mistakes: Not realising e7 reaches c6.
puzzles.hint: From e7, the knight attacks c6 and checks g8.

puzzles.prompt: Find the safe fork that wins the rook on f5.
puzzles.explanation: Ne7+ forks the king on g8 and the rook on f5 (a knight on e7 attacks f5). After the king moves, Nxf5 wins the rook.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Recognise that e7 also hits f5.
common_mistakes: Overlooking the f5 target from e7.
puzzles.hint: From e7, the knight attacks f5 — and checks g8.

puzzles.prompt: Find the safe fork that wins the queen on c6.
puzzles.explanation: Ne7+ forks the king on g8 and the queen on c6; after the king moves, Nxc6 wins the queen.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Win the queen with the e7 fork on a different square.
common_mistakes: Missing that e7 attacks c6.
puzzles.hint: Check from e7 — the queen on c6 is in range.

puzzles.prompt: The king has no g-pawn shield. Fork it and win the queen.
puzzles.explanation: Nf6+ forks the king on g8 and the queen on d5; with no g7-pawn, f6 is safe. After the king moves, Nxd5 wins the queen.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Use f6 to win the queen when the fork square is safe.
common_mistakes: Not noticing f6 hits both g8 and d5.
puzzles.hint: From e4, jump to f6: it checks the king and attacks d5.

puzzles.prompt: Find the fork that wins the rook on g6.
puzzles.explanation: Ne7+ forks the king on g8 and the rook on g6 (a knight on e7 attacks g6). After Kh8, Nxg6+ wins the rook with check.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Recognise that e7 also hits g6, winning with tempo.
common_mistakes: Overlooking the g6 target from e7.
puzzles.hint: From e7, the knight attacks g6 — and the capture comes with check.

practical_activity.name: Castled-King Fork Hunt
practical_activity.learning_objective: Find safe knight forks against a castled king in guided games.
practical_activity.setup: Students play a guided game. The trainer prompts: 'Is there a knight check on e7? Does it also hit a big piece? Is the square safe?'.
instructions: Scan for a knight check (especially e7) that also attacks a rook or queen.
Confirm the forking square is safe (not guarded by a pawn).
Play the fork and capture the piece the opponent can't save.
After the game, show one fork you found (or could have).
practical_activity.success_criteria: The student finds at least one safe knight fork against a castled king.
variations: e7 round: positions where the e7 fork wins.
Coach simul: the trainer allows castled-king fork chances.

online_practice: Solve 10 'fork' puzzles, noticing which forking square is safe.
Play a game and try to win with a knight fork against a castled king.
over_the_board: Set up the demonstrations and find the safe fork in each.
Play a game with a family member; aim for an e7 fork.
reflection_questions: Why is e7 such a good forking square against a castled king?
Why must you check whether the fork square is safe?
optional_challenge: Find a fork from one of your games and say whether the fork square was safe.

common_misconceptions: Assuming any knight check forks safely — f6/h6 are guarded by the g-pawn.
Forgetting the follow-up capture after the fork.
Not scanning for the big-piece target of the check.
typical_mistakes: Playing Nf6+ into gxf6 against a castled king.
Missing the e7 fork because the board looks busy.
Forking a square that hits only the king.
coaching_tips: Teach the e7 square explicitly: safe against f7/g7/h7 pawns, and it hits c8/c6/d5/f5/g6.
Always ask 'is the fork square safe?' before playing the knight there.
Have students name the two targets and confirm safety.
Connect to THE SCAN: scan checks for a SAFE forking square that hits a big piece.
ways_to_simplify: Start with the e7 fork against a fixed castled-king setup.
Use undefended targets so the win is clear.
Mark the forking square and check its safety together.
extensions_for_strong_students: Forks set up by a check that drives the king to g8 first.
Forks that win the queen behind a defender.
Have them compose a safe-fork puzzle against a castled king.

S115.title: Three-Move Combinations
S115.subtitle: Calculate the entire forced line to checkmate before you play move one.
S115.learning_objective: Students will calculate and execute forced three-move combinations by mapping every check and forced reply in the full line to mate before committing to move one.
expected_outcomes: Student can verbally trace a complete three-move forcing line — stating White's move, Black's only reply, and the follow-up — before touching a piece.
Student correctly identifies which opponent responses are truly forced (only legal reply, captures required, or only escape square) versus assumed.
Student recognises sacrifice as a calculated investment when the line to mate can be verified in advance, not a gamble.
Student applies THE PLAN thinking routine independently: scan for checks and captures, trace forcing sequences, confirm the final mating pattern before committing.

thinking_routine.focus: Before touching a piece, students must trace the entire three-move forcing line in their head: identify every candidate check or capture on move one, then ask 'What can my opponent actually do?' for each reply — not what they hope the opponent plays, but every legal option. A move is truly forced only when the opponent has exactly one legal or reasonable response. Students work forward through all three plies (their move, opponent's reply, their follow-up) and confirm the position is checkmate at the end. Only once the whole line is spoken or visualised to its conclusion does a student commit to move one. This discipline — calculate to the end before committing — is the defining habit of Unit 5 and the skill students will carry forward through every advanced tactics session.

materials_required: One demonstration board or projected display for guided examples
One physical chess board and set per student
Printed or projected puzzle sheets for the 8 session puzzles and 3 warm-ups
Calculation worksheet or mini whiteboard for students to record candidate lines
Timer for the guided-rapid activity (one per pair)

warmup_review.description: These three mate-in-two puzzles are a deliberate ramp: they let students re-activate the calculation habit — spotting a forcing move, then confirming the single forced reply leads to checkmate — before we extend that same chain by one more move today. Work through each one using THE PLAN: see the forcing move, name the only reply, verify the mate.

review_items.prompt: Black has a knight that can deliver check on a square that traps the white king in a corner. After the king is forced to retreat, a black rook finishes the job. Mate in two.
review_items.answer: 1...Nf3+ Kh1 2...Rb1# — the knight check forces the king to the h1 corner where it has no escape squares, and the rook slides to the back rank delivering checkmate with no possible interposition.

review_items.prompt: White can lift a rook to the h-file with check, forcing the black king to the back rank, and then a second rook move finishes on the eighth rank. Mate in two.
review_items.answer: 1.Rh5+ Kg8 2.Rh8# — the rook check pushes the king to g8 where it is hemmed in by its own pieces, and the rook swings to h8 for checkmate with no escape and no interposition available.

review_items.prompt: White has a knight that can check the black king and drive it into the corner, where a rook waiting on the g-file delivers checkmate in the Arabian pattern. Mate in two.
review_items.answer: 1.Nf6+ Kh8 2.Rg8# — the knight check forces the king to the h8 corner where the knight itself controls g8 from one direction and the rook delivers checkmate on g8, a classic Arabian-mate motif.

lesson_introduction.hook: You have already mastered the two-move combination — one forcing move, one forced reply, checkmate. Today we go one step deeper into the engine room of chess thinking: three-move forced combinations, where you must hold the entire forcing line in your mind before you touch a single piece. Welcome to Unit 5 — Advanced Tactics and Sacrifice.
lesson_introduction.narrative: A forced combination is a sequence of moves where every one of your moves puts the opponent under immediate, unavoidable pressure — a check, a capture, or a threat so powerful that there is only one reasonable reply. Because every reply is forced, you can calculate the whole line to the very end before committing, like reading a sentence all the way to the full stop before you speak. With three-move combinations that length doubles from what you know: you must visualise not one but two forced replies before you see the final checkmate appear. This is where we introduce THE PLAN as a disciplined calculation routine: before you play move one, trace every forcing move in the sequence, name the only reply the opponent can make at each step, and confirm that the final position is truly checkmate — king in check, no escape, no block, no capture of the checking piece. If the plan checks out all the way to the end, then and only then do you commit to move one.
lesson_introduction.description: This lesson opens Unit 5 by teaching students to extend their two-move calculation habit into full three-move forced lines, using THE PLAN to verify the sequence is correct before playing.

key_points: Every move in a forced combination must be a forcing move — a check, a decisive capture, or a threat that leaves the opponent with only one legal or reasonable reply.
After each of your moves, pause and visualise the opponent's forced reply before moving on — do not assume; confirm that the reply is the only one that makes sense.
At the end of the line, verify the final position is genuine checkmate: the king is in check, cannot move to any safe square, no piece can interpose, and the checking piece cannot be captured.
Count to the end before you commit to move one — a three-move combination that works for only two moves is not a combination at all, and a premature move can throw away a decisive advantage.

A three-move calculation is qualitatively different from a two-move one: you must hold two layers of forced replies in your mind simultaneously, which is why practising THE PLAN as a deliberate routine before every move one is essential at this level.
core_explanation.explanation: Calculating a forced three-move combination is the first time students must hold a branching mental picture across three plies of their own moves and two forced replies. The key discipline is ruthless honesty about what is truly forced: a move is only part of a forced combination if the opponent genuinely has no better reply. Start by scanning for forcing moves — checks and significant captures — and for each candidate ask 'what is the only thing my opponent can do here?' Visualise the resulting position, then ask the same question again for your second move and the second forced reply. Only when the line runs cleanly from move one to the final mating position, with every reply genuinely forced, should you commit. Students who rush and play move one before completing this mental check frequently find the combination falls apart on move two or three, handing the initiative back to their opponent. THE PLAN is not a slogan — it is the exact sequence of mental steps that separates a player who spots tactical patterns from one who can execute them reliably under pressure.

demonstrations.caption: Show this first, before the idea has a name: set it up, ask "what do you notice?", take two answers, and only then say what the idea is called.
demonstrations.explanation: Apply THE PLAN before touching any piece. Black's first move sacrifices the queen on b1 with check: ask yourself, can White ignore this? No — the king is in check so White must resolve it, and the only way to do so is to capture with the bishop on b1. Now visualise that resulting position and ask: what forcing move does Black have? A rook slides to c1 with check, and White's queen is the only piece that can interpose on d1 — that reply is forced. Finally, see the position after ...Qd1: Black's rook simply captures the queen on d1, and with the back rank stripped of defenders, that capture is checkmate. The entire line — queen sacrifice, rook check, rook takes blocker — is forced at every step, which is exactly why it works as a three-move combination. Answer: 1...Qxb1+ Bxb1 2...Rc1+ Qd1 3...Rxd1# — this is a queen-sacrifice deflection: Black gives up the queen to pull the bishop away from a key defensive square, then uses a forcing rook check to install a new defensive piece on the back rank that becomes the final target. Work it on the demonstration board with the class watching — this is the position the whole session is built on.

guided_discussion.description: Use these talking points to draw out students' understanding of why forced combinations work and what separates a genuine three-move forced line from a sequence that merely looks promising. Encourage students to articulate the logic in their own words rather than just nodding along.
talking_points: Ask students to explain in their own words what makes a move 'forcing' — and to give examples of moves that are NOT forcing even if they are strong.
Explore the idea of a 'forced reply': what does it mean for the opponent to have only one reasonable answer, and what happens to the combination if there are two reasonable answers?
Discuss why it is dangerous to play move one of a three-move combination before you have calculated all the way to move three — what could go wrong on move two or three?

Introduce the concept of a sacrifice in a combination: sometimes move one gives up material deliberately, and students must understand that the sacrifice only works because the opponent's capture is forced and the resulting line is pre-calculated.
Connect today's work back to the two-move combinations students already know: what is the same about the discipline required, and what is the one new mental skill that three-move combinations demand?

questions_to_ask: Before you play move one of a three-move combination, what three things do you need to confirm about the final position to be sure it is checkmate?
If your move one is a check, how do you decide which of the opponent's king moves is the forced reply — and what if the king has two possible squares?
What is the difference between a forcing move and a strong move, and why does that difference matter when you are calculating a combination?
If you calculate a three-move line and find that move two does not force a reply, is the sequence still a forced combination? What should you do instead?
Why do we say you must calculate to the END of the line before committing to move one — can you describe a situation where stopping the calculation one move early would lead you astray?
In a combination where move one involves a sacrifice, why is it essential to know your opponent's forced reply before you give up the piece?

guided_examples.prompt: Black can begin a three-move combination by driving the white king into the corner with a knight check. After the king is trapped on h1, Black sacrifices the queen to force the white rook onto g1, and then the knight delivers checkmate on f2 — a smothered mate. Mate in three.
guided_examples.walkthrough: Apply THE PLAN. Black's first move is a knight check that the white king must answer: the only legal square is h1, so that reply is forced — visualise the king on h1, surrounded by its own pieces with no escape. Now ask what forcing move Black has from that position: the queen sacrifices itself on g1 with check, and White's rook is the only piece that can resolve the check by capturing on g1 — forced. Visualise the resulting position: the white rook now sits on g1, completely sealing the king into the h1 corner. Black's knight, still active from its original check, now lands on f2, and the king has zero legal moves — every escape square is controlled and the king is hemmed in by its own rook. That is checkmate. Only because we calculated all three moves and both forced replies before committing do we know the sacrifice on move two is sound.
guided_examples.answer: 1...Nh3+ Kh1 2...Qg1+ Rxg1 3...Nf2# — this is a smothered mate: the knight drives the king into the corner, the queen lures the rook onto the very square that seals the king's last escape, and the knight delivers the final blow to a king smothered by its own pieces.

prompts: What was the most important thing we learned today? Say it in your own words.
Describe in one or two sentences what makes a reply truly 'forced' — and give one example from today's puzzles where you had to stop and check that your opponent really had no other option.
Why is a sacrifice in a forcing combination different from a mistake? How does calculating the full line to mate before you play change what a sacrifice means?
reflection.summary_line: Today's idea in one line: forced three-move combinatio — and you will use it again in every game you play from here.

puzzles.prompt: White has two rooks aimed at the back rank and the enemy queen is the only defender. The plan is a rook ladder: a check that forces the queen to block, a capture that forces the queen to block again, and a final capture that ends the game. Calculate the full forcing sequence to the end before you move. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1. Rc8+ forces the queen to block on d8 — the king has nowhere to go and the queen must interpose. 2. Rxd8+ captures that blocker with check, forcing the queen to interpose again on e8 — it is the only legal way to meet the check. 3. Rxe8# delivers mate: the rook on e8 is protected, the king cannot move, and no piece can capture or block. The queen is gone, exhausted by two forced interpositions.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Teaches students to calculate a repeating check-force-capture pattern (rook ladder) all the way to the final mating position before committing to move one.
common_mistakes: Capturing the queen immediately with the wrong rook, releasing the back-rank pressure and letting the king escape.
Stopping after the first or second capture and not verifying that the final position is actually checkmate.
puzzles.hint: Think of your two rooks as relay runners — each check hands the baton to the other by forcing a new block on the same rank.

puzzles.prompt: Black's two rooks are lined up against the first rank and White's queen is the only piece standing between them and victory. The mechanism is the same as the classic rook ladder, but now Black is the one executing it. Calculate every forced reply before you commit. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1...Rb1+ forces the white queen to block on c1 — the king is trapped on the first rank and interposition is the only legal reply. 2...Rxc1+ captures that blocker with check, forcing the queen to interpose again on d1. 3...Rxd1# delivers mate: the king cannot move, the rook on d1 is protected by its partner, and the queen has been consumed by two consecutive forced blocks.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Reinforces the rook-ladder pattern from the other side of the board, training students to recognise the mechanism regardless of which color is attacking.
common_mistakes: Playing the checks in reverse order, which gives the queen a chance to escape the ladder and survive.
Assuming the position is a draw because Black is moving first and overlooking that both rooks are already on the critical rank.
puzzles.hint: The queen must keep blocking, but each block puts her on a square where she can be captured — trace the queen's forced journey from square to square.

puzzles.prompt: White's queen and rook are both bearing down on the queenside, and the enemy king is trapped in the corner with only a rook guarding the back rank. The plan involves giving up the queen to strip that rook from its defensive post — a true sacrifice that must be calculated to the very end. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1. Qc7+ forces the king to a8 — it is the only square available in the corner. 2. Qc8+! sacrifices the queen on c8, deflecting the rook: the rook must capture on c8 because it is the only legal interposition. 3. Rxc8# — the white rook recaptures with check and the king is mated in the corner; it cannot move and there is nothing left to block or capture.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Teaches the queen-sacrifice deflection pattern: giving up the most powerful piece to remove the one defender, a calculation that requires seeing three moves deep before the sacrifice makes sense.
common_mistakes: Hesitating to sacrifice the queen because it feels wrong to give up so much material, and instead playing a quiet move that gives the opponent time to escape.
Playing the rook check first without driving the king to a8, which leaves the king an escape square and fails the combination.
puzzles.hint: Ask yourself: if you could remove the rook from c8's defence, what would happen? Then find the forcing move that makes the rook leave.

puzzles.prompt: Black has a queen and rook aimed at the e-file, and White's queen and rook are both stationed there — but Black can use the x-ray relationship between them. The plan is to force White's queen onto a square where Black's rook will already be pointing straight through it. Calculate the battery all the way to checkmate before you move. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1...Qg1+ forces the white queen to block on e1 — the king must not be exposed and interposition is the only legal reply. 2...Qxe1+ captures the blocking queen with check, forcing the white rook to recapture on e1 — it is the only way to answer the check. 3...Rxe1# — the black rook slides in behind and delivers mate; the king cannot move and no piece can interpose.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Trains students to see the x-ray battery — two pieces on the same line separated by a defender — and calculate how forcing moves can clear the middle piece and let the back piece deliver mate.
common_mistakes: Moving the rook first instead of the queen, breaking the x-ray relationship and throwing away the forced sequence.
Not noticing that after the queen exchanges, the rook is already pointing at the king with no pieces in the way.
puzzles.hint: Picture your rook waiting behind your queen — if the queen trades herself off, what is the rook looking at?

puzzles.prompt: Black's rook is on the e-file and the white queen is the only piece blocking a check from reaching the king. The plan begins with a shocking queen sacrifice that pulls the white bishop away from its defensive square, opening a forcing rook check that cannot be answered. Calculate all three moves before you commit — the sacrifice only works if the finale is forced. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1...Qxd1+! sacrifices the queen, forcing the bishop to recapture on d1 — it is the only legal way to answer the check. 2...Re1+ drives a rook check that forces the white queen to block on f1 — the king has no escape. 3...Rxf1# — the rook captures the blocking queen and the king is mated; it cannot move, capture (the rook is protected), or interpose.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Teaches the deflection sacrifice: trading the queen to drag a key defender off its post, then executing a forcing rook sequence that the opponent is powerless to stop.
common_mistakes: Playing the rook check before sacrificing the queen, which allows White to meet the check without losing the queen and the combination collapses.
Seeing the queen sacrifice but not calculating to the end and missing that the final rook check is met by a block that the rook can then capture with mate.
puzzles.hint: The bishop on d1 is holding everything together — what is the most forceful way to make it move?

puzzles.prompt: White has a knight that can deliver check and a rook ready on the c-file. The plan is to use the knight to chase the king into the corner, then bring the rook crashing in to force a block, and finally deliver a corner mate. Every move is a check — calculate all three before you start. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1. Nf6+ forces the king to h8 — it is driven into the corner with no alternative. 2. Rc8+ then delivers a rook check on the back rank, forcing the rook to block on d8 — it is the only legal interposition. 3. Rxd8# captures the blocking rook and delivers mate in the corner: the king is boxed in by its own pieces and cannot move.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Teaches the knight-and-rook coordination pattern: use the knight check to steer the king to its worst square, then bring the rook in to finish with a back-rank sequence.
common_mistakes: Playing the rook check before the knight check, which does not drive the king to the corner and gives the opponent a way to escape the follow-up.
After the king goes to h8, forgetting to check with the rook before capturing and allowing the king to slip away.
puzzles.hint: The knight can act as a shepherd — which check sends the king exactly where you want it, with no way back?

puzzles.prompt: White's rook can deliver a check that forces a piece to block — and that blocking piece will immediately be pinned against its own king by the knight that follows. The plan layers a deflection, a pin, and a capture into three consecutive forcing moves. Calculate the full sequence before you move. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1. Ra8+ forces the bishop to block on f8 — it is the only way to interpose on the back rank. 2. Ne7+ checks the king and drives it to h8, while simultaneously pinning the f8 bishop to the king — the bishop cannot move to capture or block. 3. Rxf8# — the rook captures the pinned bishop with mate: the king is in the corner, the bishop is pinned and cannot move, and there are no other escape squares.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Teaches students to combine a deflection move with a pin in a three-move sequence, calculating how one forcing move can set up a pin that makes the final capture unstoppable.
common_mistakes: Playing the knight check before the rook check, which does not place a pinned piece on f8 and leaves the king with a way to avoid mate.
Not recognising that the bishop on f8 will be absolutely pinned after the knight check, and therefore thinking the combination fails because the bishop could capture.
puzzles.hint: After the first rook check forces a block, ask yourself: which piece can deliver a check that also freezes that blocker in place?

puzzles.prompt: White has a rook and a pawn on the seventh rank, and the enemy rook is the only piece that can try to hold the back rank. The plan forces the enemy rook to block two consecutive checks, and on the third move a pawn promotes — delivering checkmate on the spot. Calculate every forced reply before you push. Mate in three.
puzzles.explanation: 1. Rd8+ forces the knight to block on e8 — it is the only legal interposition. 2. Rxe8+ captures the knight with check, forcing the rook to block on g8 — the king is trapped and interposition is the only reply. 3. hxg8=Q# — the pawn promotes to a queen with check and it is checkmate: the king is hemmed in, the newly promoted queen controls the escape squares, and there is no capture or block available.
puzzles.educational_purpose: Teaches students to calculate a forcing sequence that ends with a pawn promotion to checkmate, combining back-rank tactics with the transformative power of promotion.
common_mistakes: Promoting the pawn immediately without first clearing the back rank with rook checks, which allows the opponent to capture the new queen.
After the first rook check and block, exchanging rooks voluntarily instead of capturing the blocking piece with check to keep the sequence forcing.
puzzles.hint: Your pawn is one step from promotion, but the back rank is guarded — can two rook checks clear the path and force a block exactly where the promoted queen will deliver mate?

practical_activity.name: Calculate-Out-Loud Combination Game
practical_activity.learning_objective: Students practise verbalising a complete three-move forcing line to their partner before executing it on the board, reinforcing the habit of calculating to the end before committing.
practical_activity.setup: Students work in pairs at a shared board. The coach or a student sets up a puzzle position from the session (starting with P1–P2 Foundation positions). Before either player touches a piece, the solver must state the full three-move line out loud — 'I play this, you must play that, then I play this and it is checkmate' — so their partner can listen for any gap in the calculation. Partners rotate solver and checker roles after each puzzle.
instructions: Set up the assigned puzzle position. The solver studies the board in silence for up to 90 seconds, identifying checks, captures, and forced replies — no piece is touched during calculation.

The solver speaks the full line aloud before moving: state move one, state the forced reply (and why it is the only option), state move two, state the forced reply, state move three, and confirm checkmate. Partner listens and flags any moment the line branches or an opponent reply is skipped.

Only after the partner agrees the line is complete does the solver execute the moves on the board. If the spoken line reaches checkmate as stated, the pair earns the point and the partner takes over as solver for the next position.

If the spoken line contains a hole — an unaddressed opponent reply or a move that does not actually force the response claimed — the partner identifies the flaw before any pieces are moved, and the solver has one further 60-second think to correct and re-state the line from the start.
practical_activity.success_criteria: Both partners can state a complete, gapless three-move forcing line for at least three positions — correctly identifying why each opponent reply is forced — before executing a single move on the board.
variations: Speed round: once a pair is comfortable, reduce the silent calculation window to 60 seconds per puzzle to simulate tournament time pressure.
Blind calculation: the solver closes their eyes after a 20-second study period and must state the full line from memory, building internal visualisation before returning to the board to verify.

Partner challenge mode: after the solver states the line, the partner picks one ply and plays a different 'what if' move; the solver must show why that deviation loses faster or no faster than the main line.
Board rotation: every two puzzles the pair switches to a different board station so students encounter fresh positions and cannot rely on short-term position memory.

online_practice: Complete five mate-in-three puzzles on Lichess (puzzle storm or puzzle practice, filter by 'Mate in 3'). Before clicking each move, write or say aloud the full three-move line; aim for at least three clean first-attempt solves.

Play three short games (10+0 or 15+0) on Lichess or Chess.com. After each game, use the engine analysis to find one moment where a forced combination existed and reconstruct the full line in the move list.
over_the_board: Replay one of today's P6–P8 Challenge puzzles from memory — set up the start position without looking at the sheet, then calculate and execute the three-move line. Ask a family member or friend to play Black's moves as you call them out.

Set up the queen-sacrifice back-ranker from the guided example and show it to someone at home, explaining every forced reply out loud as if coaching them. This rehearsal of the explanation deepens the calculation habit.
reflection_questions: Describe in one or two sentences what makes a reply truly 'forced' — and give one example from today's puzzles where you had to stop and check that your opponent really had no other option.
Why is a sacrifice in a forcing combination different from a mistake? How does calculating the full line to mate before you play change what a sacrifice means?
optional_challenge: Find a real game (from any source: a tournament database, a famous game book, or a YouTube analysis video) that contains a forced mate-in-three. Write down the position, the full three-move line, and one sentence explaining why Black's replies are forced at each step — bring it to the next session to share.

common_misconceptions: Students frequently confuse 'check' with 'forced': giving check is not the same as giving a forced reply. Opponents can sometimes interpose, block, or escape in unexpected ways. Stress that 'forced' means the reply is the ONLY legal or reasonable option after checking all defensive resources.

Many students believe a sacrifice is risky by definition. In a forced combination the sacrifice is not a guess — it is a statement: 'I calculated the whole line and there is nothing you can do.' Reinforce that the plan is validated before the piece is given up, turning sacrifice from instinct into craft.

Students often stop calculating after they find a plausible continuation rather than the only continuation. They assume the opponent will cooperate. Push back gently: 'What if they play something else here?' — this habit of challenging their own line is the single biggest leap in calculation quality.
typical_mistakes: Playing move one of the combination before fully tracing moves two and three, then discovering mid-sequence that the forced reply they assumed is not actually forced — leading to a collapsed combination or a blunder.

Miscounting ply: students sometimes describe a two-move sequence as 'three moves' because they count each individual move rather than tracking White's moves and Black's replies as separate plies. Use the language 'White plays, Black replies, White plays, Black replies, White plays — checkmate' to make the five-ply structure explicit.

Overlooking quiet defensive resources — particularly interpositions and double-blocking moves that are not checks or captures and therefore easy to miss in candidate generation. Encourage students to ask 'Can Black block or interpose at any point in the line?' as a checklist step.
coaching_tips: When a student finds the first move quickly, slow them down with 'Great — now tell me the whole story before you touch it.' The pause for verbalisation catches more errors than any amount of board study.

Use the warm-up mate-in-twos at the very start of session to calibrate the room: which students breeze through them and are ready for the core puzzles, and which students still benefit from the two-move frame before extending to three. Do not rush the transition for students who are not yet fluent at two-move calculation.

For P3 (queen sacrifice) and P5 (deflection sacrifice), ask 'What is Black not able to do after you give up your queen/piece?' before any move is played. This question trains students to verify the opponent's loss of defensive resource, which is the conceptual heart of a sacrifice combination.

During the guided examples, model imperfect calculation: start a line, realise move three does not deliver mate, back up aloud, and restart. Showing students that even strong players check and revise their lines — rather than seeing the answer instantly — normalises the process and reduces anxiety about not seeing it 'immediately'.
ways_to_simplify: Reduce the combination length temporarily: for students struggling with three-ply calculation, return to a mate-in-two from the warm-up set and add one extra forcing move on top, turning it into a 'two-plus-one' rather than an abstract three-mover. The continuity makes the extension feel incremental.

Restrict the puzzle set to P1–P2 (rook ladders) for the entire practical activity. Rook ladders have maximally forced replies — there is almost never an alternative for the defending king — so students experience genuine three-move calculation without the extra cognitive load of evaluating defensive resources.

Allow partner collaboration during the activity: two students calculate together before one speaks the line, sharing the candidate-generation load. Transition to solo calculation once confidence grows.
extensions_for_strong_students: After solving each puzzle, ask the student to find the best defensive try — the one move that makes the combination hardest, even if it does not refute it — and explain why it still fails. This anti-refutation analysis is the hallmark of advanced calculation.

Challenge the student to construct an original mate-in-three position on a blank board using only the piece types from one of today's puzzles. The construction task reverses the cognitive direction: instead of finding a line, they must build a position where exactly one three-move line works.

Introduce the concept of a decoy sacrifice: a move that gives up material to deflect a defending piece away from a key square, enabling a mating pattern that would otherwise be covered. Ask students to identify which of today's puzzles contain a decoy and which contain a different sacrifice type, and to articulate the distinction.

This session opens Unit 5 'Advanced Tactics and Sacrifice', so its primary goal is establishing THE PLAN as a non-negotiable habit, not maximising puzzle throughput. Allocate roughly 8–10 minutes to the two guided examples (queen-sacrifice back-ranker and smothered mate), ensuring students verbalise the full line for both — do not simply show the moves. The three warm-up mate-in-twos should take no more than 6 minutes and serve as a calculation ramp. In the puzzle set, P1–P2 (rook ladders) are Foundation and should be accessible to all; use them to set the standard for 'speak the whole line before you move.' P3–P5 (queen sacrifice, x-ray/battery, deflection) are Core and are where most of the teaching energy belongs. P6–P8 (corner mate, deflection+pin, promotion) are Challenge and are intended for students who finish the core set cleanly; do not feel pressure to get every student through P8 in session one of the unit. The skill of calculating forced lines to the end before committing is the central thread that every subsequent Unit 5 session will review forward; plant it firmly here even at the cost of puzzle quantity.

S115.author: Lead Curriculum Author
